summary.title: Learning Parser Combinators With Rust
summary.one_liner: You learn to build a parser from scratch in Rust using parser combinators, starting from a simple function type and building up to a small XML-like parser.
takeaways: A parser is a function taking input and returning either the parsed output plus the remaining input, or an error.
Small parsers (literal match, identifier) can be combined with combinators such as pair, left, right and map.
map works as a functor: it changes a parser's result type while keeping its structure.
A Parser trait with a type alias for ParseResult makes parser signatures shorter and extensible.
Rust specifics matter: string slices, UTF-8 byte indexing, and Unicode-aware char methods like is_alphabetic.
summary.summary: The article is a hands-on tutorial for Rust programmers who want to understand parser combinators from first principles, with no external dependencies. It builds a parser for a simplified XML subset that produces an Element struct with name, attributes and children. It starts with a basic function type over &str, then writes a single-character parser, a literal-match builder, and an identifier parser, with tests for each. It then introduces the pair combinator, map as a functor, a ParseResult type alias, and a Parser trait. The page text ends partway through the trait section, so later combinators are not covered in this excerpt.
